extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, legislators, jurists, and scholars of comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and comparative principles about how different forms of government (despotism, monarchy, republic) should organize succession, public office, laws, trials, punishments, gifts, rewards, and administrative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession by fundamental law
rubrics_metrics.description: When succession is established by a fundamental law, a single prince is the successor and his brothers have no real or apparent right to dispute the crown; one cannot presume or assert a particular will of the father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a legal, fixed succession stops intrigues and ambition, removes motives to murder or detain rivals, and stabilizes the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of royal brothers in despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotic states the prince's brothers are both slaves and rivals; prudence therefore requires securing their persons (imprisonment or worse) since religion in some regions treats victory as God's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains why in despotisms rulers often neutralize potential claimants — a structural feature rather than mere cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism and familial structure (marriage, polygamy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Despot rulers habitually take many wives (especially in Asia) and have many children, producing weak familial affections and a reigning family that appears large but amounts to nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large polygamous households reduce parental affection and increase palace intrigue; examples (Artaxerxes) are cited to show how such arrangements foster conspiracy or justify extreme reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate and legal majority
rubrics_metrics.description: In warm climates where despotism reigns, passions and maturation occur earlier; people marry younger and can reach legal majority sooner (e.g., in Turkey majority begins at fifteen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers should account for social and climatic differences when setting ages of majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cession of goods as feature of moderate governments
rubrics_metrics.description: Cession of goods (cession de biens) is natural in moderate governments and especially republics because of greater trust in citizens’ probity; it was instituted in Rome (lex Julia) to avoid prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The availability of cession avoids ignominious penalties (e.g., prison) and mitigates civil unrest caused by debt and confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of cession and insecurity in despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotisms cession of goods cannot happen because fortunes are insecure and one lends to persons rather than property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This leads to high interest rates and discourages large-scale commerce; merchants live hand-to-mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usury naturalized under despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Poverty and uncertainty of fortunes in despotisms naturalize usury: lenders increase prices proportionally to the risk of lending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic policies in despotisms must account for the capital scarcity and compensatory high interest that restricts commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited commercial law in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws on commerce have little place in despotisms; they reduce essentially to mere police regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the sovereign monopolizes or dominates trade, complex commercial regulation is unnecessary and often unused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peculation (embezzlement) as expected in despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Where government is unjust and arbitrary, those who must administer it will use it for themselves; peculation becomes a normal crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because embezzlement is ordinary, confiscations can be politically useful in despotisms to console the people and raise revenue that would be difficult to levy directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confiscations appropriate in despotisms but harmful in moderates
rubrics_metrics.description: Confiscations are useful in despotic states (consolation and revenue) but in moderate states they would render property insecure, impoverish innocent heirs, and destroy equality in republics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In republics and monarchies confiscation should be sharply limited—historical Roman law limited confiscation principally to crimes of lèse-majesté.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit confiscation to serious crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often wise to follow the Roman spirit and restrict confiscations to certain crimes (e.g., lèse-majesté); where local custom governs property, confiscate only acquests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bodin’s suggestion: in jurisdictions with local property customs, confine confiscation to acquests to preserve customary property rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration vs distribution of power
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotism power passes entirely to the person entrusted (the vizir is the despot himself); in monarchy the monarch tempers power when granting it — he gives authority but retains a greater part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of offices should reflect whether the regime seeks to create intermediate powers (monarchy) or centralize all authority (despotism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachment of extended-command officers in monarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: In many monarchies those with extended command are not attached to a permanent militia corps, so their command depends on the prince's will and they lack an independent power base.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents the emergence of men 'great by themselves' — a structural safeguard incompatible with despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of magistrates on known law
rubrics_metrics.description: In monarchies and moderates the law is known and magistrates can follow it; in despotisms where law is the prince’s will, magistrates cannot follow an unknown will and must instead follow their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, published law is necessary to enable magistrates to act predictably; lack of known law makes subordinate officials into arbiters of the sovereign’s will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gifts/presents as social lubricant in despotisms
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotisms one may not approach a superior without an offering; gifts corrupt favors and even kings may not receive petitions without presents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom normalizes gift-giving (even by the poor), corrupts justice, and substitutes material patronage for civic rights — odious in republics, less so in monarchies where honor competes with gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small permitted presents lead to escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing magistrates to accept small presents creates desire for more; those who take a little are soon convinced to take more, with excuses proliferating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato recommended harsh penalties (death) for magistrates taking gifts; Roman law allowing small gifts was criticized as fostering corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of sovereign rewards by regime
rubrics_metrics.description: In despotisms sovereigns reward by honors that lead to fortune (material benefits); in republics the state rewards by testimonies of virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The form of rewards reflects the regime’s motivating principle: material inducements in despotism, moral honor in republics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large rewards signal regime decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Generous largesse by the state (big rewards) is a sign of decline in monarchies and republics; the best emperors were frugal and relied on 'treasure of honor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive material rewards corrode the force of honor and civic virtue; moderation is a sign of healthy institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to accept public office in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should compel citizens to accept public offices in republican governments because magistracies are deposits of virtue and duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In monarchies offices are honors and hence properly optional; punitive examples exist (Venice punished refusals by exile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to accept lower military rank in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: In republics a citizen may be obliged to accept a lower military position than previously held, because virtue demands continual self-sacrifice for the state; monarchies and honor systems resist such degradation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Republican military ethos treats service as duty tied to citizenship; monarchies treat rank as honor incompatible with demotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union vs separation of civil and military offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil and military offices should be united in a republic and separated in a monarchy: republics must avoid a permanent military estate, monarchies must prevent soldiers from holding civil power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniting roles in republics reinforces citizen-soldier identity; separating them in monarchies limits abuse by those possessing both civil trust and military force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venality (sale) of offices by regime
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale of offices (vénalité) should not exist in despotisms (where instant appointment/removal is needed), can be appropriate in monarchies to make offices quasi-hereditary and stable, and is condemned by philosophers of virtuous republics (Plato).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In monarchies venality channels ambition into family professions of office and encourages industry; in republics it undermines virtue and merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for censors in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: Republics require censors to correct moeurs, punish negligence and prevent corrupt examples that elude the law and weaken civic virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Censors police moral and civic norms beyond criminal law; monarchy’s honor functions as an informal censor, and despotism lacks need (or capacity) for censors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of civil law in monarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchies cannot have laws as simple as despotisms; they need tribunals, preserved decisions (jurisprudence), many rules and distinctions because of ranks and varied property categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal complexity reflects necessary administration of honor, property types (propre/acquêts/dotaux etc.), and privileges; the monarch can tolerate and even craft such nuances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of civil law in despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotisms have very few civil laws concerning land, succession, commerce, or dowries because the sovereign owns the land, succeeds by right, monopolizes trade, and controls marriage of enslaved women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because most will lacks independence, many moral actions are resolved by patriarchs/masters rather than courts; travelers rarely report civil law in despotic lands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of criminal procedure in despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotisms resolve disputes promptly by rough means (pacha may mete out corporal punishment); the manner of ending disputes is indifferent so long as they end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick procedures minimize litigation but sacrifice protections for life, honor, and property; heavy reliance on witnesses and corporal punishments is noted in Oriental practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural formalities as protection of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalities, delays, costs, and pains of justice in moderate governments are the price citizens pay for liberty and security of life, honor, and property; reducing them risks arbitrary power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the law is protective of citizens, lengthy procedures are justifiable as safeguards; simplifying justice for expedience erodes freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to judge by precise text vs spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: The closer a government is to a republic, the more judges must follow the precise text of law; in monarchies judges can seek the spirit where the text is ambiguous; in despotisms the judge is his own rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting 'consult the spirit of the law' as an axiom is dangerous as it opens the law to arbitrary subjective interpretations (Beccaria quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of judgments and deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: In monarchies judges deliberate, reconcile opinions, and act like arbiters; in republics judges (or juries) give simple verdicts without mutual modification (absoudre/condamner/non liquet); Romans used fixed formulae to present a single fact to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial procedures should fit the constitutional form: collective deliberation suits monarchies, single-fact presentation and fixed actions suit republican popular judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on popular judgment and protections
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent abuse by popular tribunals, Rome allowed exile before judgment and dedicated condemned goods to sacred use; review mechanisms (e.g., Solon’s review by the Areopagus) could correct popular error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural safeguards (lenteur, review, ability to exile) are recommended to temper passion and secure fair judgment when the people judge crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of arbitrary interpretation of law
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on a judge’s notion of the 'spirit' of the law risks making the law mutable by individual reason, moods, or relations, producing inconsistent punishments across times and tribunals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stable, published laws and limitations on discretionary interpretation are necessary to prevent caprice and protect citizens’ rights.
